notes.heading: Particles inside the nuclear atom
points: Rutherford's model: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus holds over 99.9% of the atom's mass; electrons are held outside by electrostatic attraction.
Nucleus holds protons and neutrons (nucleons). Relative mass: proton 1, neutron 1, electron negligible.
Relative charge: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1. Electrons are outside the nucleus.
Actual masses and charges of the particles are given in the data booklet.
The atom's diameter is about 100000 times the nucleus's diameter, so most of an atom is empty space.

notes.heading: Nuclear symbol: protons, neutrons, electrons
points: In the symbol (A over Z, then X), A is the mass number, Z the atomic number, X the element symbol.
Z = number of protons. A = Z + N, so neutrons N = A − Z.
In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.
In an ion, electrons = protons − charge. Mg2+ (Z = 12): 12 protons, 10 electrons. O2−: 8 protons, 10 electrons.
Example: gold-197 (Z = 79) has 79 protons, 118 neutrons and 79 electrons.

notes.heading: Isotopes and their properties
points: Isotopes are atoms of one element with the same Z but different neutron numbers, so different mass numbers.
Same electron number gives similar chemical properties, e.g. chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
Physical properties differ because the masses differ: density, melting point and boiling point (e.g. 1H2O vs 2H2O).
Differences in physical properties allow isotope enrichment, e.g. raising the 235U proportion for reactor fuel.
Isotopes can be written as 37Cl, chlorine-37 or Cl-37; the atomic number is optional since the symbol fixes it.

notes.heading: Relative atomic mass from isotope data
points: Ar is the weighted average mass number of an element's isotopes, so it is not a whole number.
Ar = Σ(mass number × abundance %) ÷ 100.
With two isotopes and a known Ar, let x = % of one isotope and 100 − x the other, then solve for x.
Using mass numbers gives a slightly different answer from the true Ar, because mass numbers are rounded masses.

notes.heading: Mass spectra and relative atomic mass
points: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (intensity) against m/z for the ions detected.
Atoms are vaporized and ionized to 1+ ions, then accelerated and deflected by a magnetic field. Uncharged particles are not detected.
Lower m and higher charge z means more deflection. Lighter ions are deflected most.
Read each peak's m/z (the isotope's mass number) and its abundance, then Ar = Σ(m/z × abundance) ÷ total abundance.
Example: boron peaks at 10 (19.9%) and 11 (80.1%) give Ar = 10.8.
Operational details of the spectrometer are not assessed.

definitions.definition: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.
definitions.trap: Saying 'elements' instead of 'atoms', or reversing it to different protons, same neutrons.

definitions.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with mass number, which counts protons plus neutrons.

definitions.definition: The total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in the nucleus of an atom.
definitions.trap: Defining it by molar mass, or as the number of protons only.

definitions.definition: The weighted average mass of an element's naturally occurring isotopes, relative to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
definitions.trap: Giving a simple average of the isotope masses, ignoring abundance.

definitions.definition: The percentage of the atoms of an element found on Earth that are a particular isotope.
definitions.trap: Giving a percentage of mass or of compounds instead of atoms of that element.

definitions.definition: The mass of an ion divided by its charge, which decides how much it is deflected in the mass spectrometer.
definitions.trap: Treating m/z as mass alone; for 1+ ions it equals the mass number.
